title: How to Humanize Your Classroom or School When You're Teaching from a Distance -distance-principles-and-practices
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In one of his most comprehensive distance-learning pieces, Dave Stuart Jr. lays out five grounding principles and a set of concrete practices for humanizing an online classroom. Drawing on philosopher Dallas Willard's claim that human beings are largely "hidden" beings, Stuart argues that humane classrooms are ones where students feel valued, known, respected, and safe — and that both the difficulty and the possibility of building such spaces persist, even intensified, in online settings. He then presents Michelle Pacansky-Brock's three-part framework — cultivating human presence, identifying "high opportunity" students, and practicing warm-demander pedagogy — with specific practices under each, including introductory story videos, imperfect instructional videos, video postcards, audio feedback, and targeted first-week surveys. Stuart closes candidly acknowledging how exhausting this work feels relative to in-person teaching, while insisting it remains both necessary and achievable one step at a time.
points: Stuart's five grounding principles culminate in the claim that humanizing online spaces is difficult but "completely possible," invoking the Stockdale Paradox of facing brutal facts while remaining optimistic.
Pacansky-Brock's three-part framework — cultivate human presence, identify high-opportunity students, be a warm demander — organizes the piece's practical recommendations.

"High opportunity" students are identified through a first-week survey targeting how a student feels about the class and what's most likely to interfere with their success, enabling efficient, targeted outreach rather than blanket effort.

Warm-demander pedagogy, rooted in Kleinfeld's 1975 and Baumrind's 1966 research, is framed as the combination of high support and high challenge needed to move students from dependent to independent learners.
quotes: Human beings are invisible creatures, Willard claimed, in the sense that we have bodies, which are visible, but these bodies are only a fraction of what a human is.
A humane classroom or school is a place where students feel warmly seen — like they are known, valued, and respected — and feel like it is unnecessary to remain invisible.
It's the Stockdale Paradox: prisoner-of-war Jim Stockdale's observation that the prisoners most likely to survive were both realistic ("I'm in hell") and optimistic ("I will prevail").

But while it's not necessary to make sure that all of the videos in our online courses are made by us, it is hugely helpful (from a humanization standpoint) to make many of them from scratch. And they need not be perfect!
Michelle Pacansky-Brock recommends using a short survey in week one "to illuminate the psychological barriers and real-life scenarios that may interfere with your students' success.

The idea of warm demander pedagogy is that in a humanized space where relationships are strong, the most effective instructors challenge students to push themselves and grow from dependent to independent learners.

Even though the practices above are all aimed at high-leverage, high-efficiency intervention, it still looks like work and change and exhaustion compared to those bustling hallways and flesh-and-blood relationships that I started the post with.
